faq.q: Where does the dust come from?
faq.a: Mostly from comets, which shed dust as they warm near the Sun, with some from collisions between asteroids. The grains slowly spiral into the Sun, so new dust keeps replacing them.
asks: What makes the zodiacal dust cloud?

faq.a: Countless tiny dust grains between the planets scatter sunlight. One grain is invisible, but together they make a faint glow that is brightest near the Sun.
asks: What makes the zodiacal light shine?

faq.q: When can you see zodiacal light?
faq.a: From a very dark place with no Moon. In the northern hemisphere, look west about an hour after sunset from February to April, or east before dawn from September to November, when the zodiac stands steeply up from the horizon.
asks: Where should I look for zodiacal light?

faq.q: Why is it called zodiacal light?
faq.a: Because it stretches along the zodiac, the band of constellations that the Sun, Moon and planets appear to travel through. That band marks the flat plane of the Solar System.
It is an old name for zodiacal light seen before sunrise. The faint cone in the east can look like the first glow of morning, but it appears while the real dawn is still an hour or more away.
asks: Why is zodiacal light called false dawn?

facts: Zodiacal light is sunlight scattered by interplanetary dust lying in the plane of the Solar System.
In the northern hemisphere, zodiacal light is best seen after dusk in spring and before dawn in autumn.
Zodiacal light seen before sunrise is often called the false dawn.
